newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM Simitis wins mandate, chooses cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM Simitis wins mandate, chooses cabinet.

text.p: Triumphant socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis rolled up his sleeves on Monday vowing to change the face of Greece and bring the European Union's poorest member in line with its partners.
Bolstered by a strong election victory on Sunday, the unassuming technocrat will soon name a cabinet to tackle Greece's chronic economic problems by implementing disciplined, pro-European policies.
"I will announce my new cabinet in the next few days," he told reporters after receiving a mandate to form a government within three days from President Costis Stephanopoulos.
With his hands freed by a new four-year term, Simitis is expected to ignore in-party politicking and name a fresh and more efficient cabinet firmly bearing his personal stamp.
Simitis has made clear he wants to reinvent Greece's image, changing it from that of an indebted Balkan backwater to a modern European country with a competitive economy.

"My partners and I have the huge responsibility of leading Greece into the 21st century," he said after winning Sunday's poll. "Today's victory belongs to all those lively and creative forces who believe in the competitiveness of the Greek economy."
In stark contrast to his late mentor Andreas Papandreou, who scored three landslide socialist election wins on populist, free-spending pledges, Simitis promised diligent, hard work.

"He is methodical and has a step-by-step approach," a Western diplomat told Reuters. "He has done an exceptional job in his first eight months by reknitting tattered relations with the European Union and the United States."
Socialist party sources said he would like to retain his economic ministers to signal stability to the financial markets, which welcomed the victory.
National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, who sharply cut chronic double-digit inflation to 8.5 percent in August, was expected to continue to work towards Greece's EU targets.
Next year he must curb public hiring and cut spending by $1.2 billion to trim the public debt.

Simitis also wants to keep Finance Minister Alexandros Papadopoulos, who proved an effective tax collector and must tackle a big deficit in next year's budget, but may not be able to convince him to remain in one of Greece's hardest ministries.

Education Minister George Papandreou, son of the late socialist leader, is a possible replacement for Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos, notorious for offending Greece's allies with his frank comments.

With almost all votes counted on Monday the socialists had 41.5 percent of the vote and 162 deputies in the 300-seat parliament compared to the New Democracy conservatives who won 38.17 percent of the vote and 108 deputies.
New Democracy leader Miltiadis Evert swiftly resigned after his defeat. The succession battle in his party is sure to weaken opposition to Simitis's policies.
